newsitem.title: QATAR: Qatar signs petrochemical deal with Chiyoda.
newsitem.headline: Qatar signs petrochemical deal with Chiyoda.

text.p: Japan's Chiyoda Corp on Monday signed a $425 million engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) contract to build a petrochemical plant for Qatar Fuel Additives Company, senior Qatari officials said.
The overall cost of the scheme is $650 million.

"The project will be funded by a mix of export credits, commercial loan and equity contribution," Qatar's Minister of Energy and Industry Abdullah bin Hamad al-Attiyah after signing the deal with a representative of the Janapese firm.
It will produce 850,000 tonnes of methonol and 620,000 tonnes of the environmentally friendly methyl tertiary butyl ether (MTBE) a year as of mid-1999, he told reporters.

Qatar Fuel Additives Company, or Qafac, is a 50-50 joint venture between the state's Qatar General Petroleum Corporation (QGPC) and three foreign partners. They are Chinese Petroleum Corporation (CPC) of Taiwan, which holds 20 percent, the private Lee Chang Yung Chemical Industry Corporation of Taiwan (LCYCIC) and Canada's International Octane Ltd (IOL) that hold 15 percent each.
Both CPC and LCYCIC have laced their equity participation with an offer to buy a third of QAFAC's production on a long term basis.

Four international engineering firms were bidding for the contract. But Chiyoda won the deal over France's Technip, America's Fluor Daniel and Japan Gasoline Corporation (JGC) because of a "more attractive financial package it had submitted with its offer," an official said.
Qafac is one of the oil and gas-rich state's four petrochemical projects designed to cash in on its massive gas reserves - the third largest in the world after those in Russia and Iran.
The first, Qatar Petrochemicals Company, has been producing since 1982 and a partnership deal for a Qatar Vinyl Company was signed up early this month with Norwegian and French firms.
Qafac is more advanced of a similar project, Qatar Clean Energy Company (Qacenco), a joint venture of QGPC and Britain's Penspen International.
Little has emerged about Qacenco's progress since its third partner - Petronas of Malaysia - withdrew its 25 percent stake in the company last June.
But Attiyah has vowed to make it "a success" by turning over Petronas's shares to another partner or partners "in due course."
